svg.text: BEST FOR: WHICH AGENT PATTERN TO USE
FORMAT LINEAGE: Anthropic, Building effective agents (Dec 2024)
Six Ways to Wire an LLM — and the One Question That Picks the Right One
Anthropic's advice after a year with dozens of teams: the best systems used simple, composable patterns, not frameworks. Pick the simplest one that fits.
gate = programmatic check between steps (e.g. 'is the outline on-brief?')
The task splits into fixed, ordered steps and you trade a little
latency for higher accuracy on each step.
Steps are not predictable, or one call already does the job well.
Write marketing copy → programmatic check it fits the brief →
translate it. The gate stops bad drafts early.
Inputs fall into distinct categories that are handled better by
Categories blur together — a misroute is worse than one general
Support: refunds, technical, general each get a specialist prompt;
easy questions go to a small, cheap model.
Independent subtasks (sectioning) or you want several opinions
Subtasks depend on each other's output.
One model answers while a guardrail model screens the input; three
dashed = subtasks are decided at run time, not hard-coded
You cannot predict the subtasks up front — a central LLM decides
Subtasks are known ahead of time (use parallelization — it is
A coding change that touches an unknown set of files: the
orchestrator picks files, workers edit each one.
loop until the evaluator says 'meets the bar' (or max rounds)
You have clear evaluation criteria and iterating on feedback
There is no reliable way to judge the output.
Literary translation: one model drafts, a critic flags lost
nuance, repeat until the critic is satisfied.
stop on: task complete, max steps, or a human checkpoint
Open-ended problems where you can't script the path, in a trusted
environment with ground-truth feedback (tests, tool results).
A workflow would do; cost, latency, and compounding errors are
SWE-bench-style coding: edit until the tests pass; stop at max
Ask first: can I predict the steps? Yes → a workflow (1-5). No, and I can verify results → an agent (6). Start simple; add complexity only when it measurably helps.
